title: Lalita's hymn of names
hookLine: a hymn that opens with names, and never stops naming
carry: in a sahasranama, saying the name is the prayer
tomorrow: what if the Sita who was carried off wasn't really Sita?
last: A GODDESS OUT OF THE FIRE.

lines: HOW ARE YOU SAVED IN THEIR PHONES?
cards: Look at how different people have you saved in their phones. A parent has one name for you. A best friend, another.
A grandmother might have five, depending on her mood. Here's an old hymn that does that on purpose. It opens: Shri Mata.
Shri Maharajni. Shrimat Simhasaneshvari. Then another name, and another, on and on.
No story told in sentences, no request at the end. Just names. It's the Lalita Sahasranama, and tradition places it in the Brahmanda Purana, right after yesterday's story.

teach.b: First clue: listen to what the names say. Shri Mata: the holy mother. Shri Maharajni: the great queen.
Shrimat Simhasaneshvari: the queen on the lion throne. Then two names that are yesterday's story, folded small. Chidagni kunda sambhuta: born from the fire pit of consciousness.
Deva karya samudyata: risen to do the work of the gods. So the names carry the story. Someone who knows the Lalitopakhyana hears the whole battle inside a few words.
The frame is the same, too: Hayagriva teaches Agastya, and tradition says the names were first sung by goddesses of speech, at Lalita's own command.

teach.h: A NAME IS SAID TO SOMEONE.
teach.b: Second clue: a name is said to someone. A description talks about a person; a name turns toward her.

teach.h: MOTHER, QUEEN, GIRL FROM THE FIRE.
teach.b: Each one faces one more side of the same goddess: mother, queen, the girl who rose from the fire. Third clue: said one after another, the names add up to a portrait no single sentence could hold.
That's the answer, and it's one of the oldest Hindu practices: saying the names of God. There are hymns of names for Vishnu and for Shiva too, and many families say one at home.
For the people who say them, the names aren't praise with the content left out.

teach.h: SAYING THE NAME IS THE PRAYER.
teach.b: Saying the name is the prayer. Some devotees recite the whole hymn; some keep a few names close and come back to them.

how: Many devotees of the goddess recite the Lalita Sahasranama, the hymn of her names, at home or in temples, some daily and some on festival days; others keep a few of its names for quiet repetition. Hymns of names for Vishnu and Shiva are recited the same way.

games.why: in the Lalita Sahasranama the names are the content: mother, queen, born from the fire of consciousness. each one turns toward a face of the same goddess.

practice: Say three of today's names out loud, slowly, the way devotees do: Shri Mata. Shri Maharajni. Shrimat Simhasaneshvari.
Leave a full breath between each, and let each one turn you toward a different face: mother, queen, the one on the lion throne.
If you don't pray, say instead the names the people who love you call you, and notice that none of them cancels the others.
